notes.meaning: Eliphaz has just finished his long speech telling Job to turn back to God. Job listened without cutting in. Now he answers him. He still defends his complaints and says Eliphaz's arguments were weak.

Job wishes someone fair could put his grief on one side of a scale and his troubles on the other. His troubles would weigh more than all the sand of the sea, too many to count and too heavy to measure. That is why his earlier words were rash. He is not saying he was right to say them. He is asking his friends to understand why he spoke that way.

Job feels as if God Himself is shooting poisoned arrows into him. The poison seems to soak into his very spirit, and God's terrors line up against him like an army. The worst pain is not his losses or his sores. It is the feeling that the God he loves is now against him. Matthew Henry and Wesley see in this a picture of Jesus, who felt the deepest pain in His soul when He bore our sins.

A wild donkey doesn't bray, and an ox doesn't moo, when it has plenty of good food. They only cry out when something is wrong. In the same way, Job is not complaining for no reason. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adds that a person should still show a better spirit than an animal.

Nobody enjoys bland food with no salt, or the slimy white of an egg. Job says his life now feels like eating food he would once have refused to touch. Many read this as describing his sufferings, which he must swallow every day. Others, including Matthew Henry and Enduring Word, also hear Job saying that Eliphaz's words of comfort tasted flat and gave him no strength.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars say no one is sure what substance the phrase "white of an egg" really means. Job's disgust is plain either way.

notes.meaning: Job asks God again to let him die, as he did in chapter 3. God had held back His hand and only let Job's body be wounded. Now Job wants God to let His hand go and cut his life off, like a weaver cutting finished cloth from the loom. Job never thinks of taking his own life. Matthew Henry and the Geneva Notes say this wish was still wrong, because it asked God for something that was not His will.

Even in endless pain, Job has one comfort. He has not turned his back on the words of God, the Holy One. This answers Eliphaz's hint that Job was a fake. With a clear conscience, Job is not afraid to die. He says he would even be glad of sharp pain if it brought death sooner.

Eliphaz told Job he could still have good days ahead. Job says he has no strength left to hope for that. He is not made of stone or bronze. He is flesh and blood like everyone else, and he cannot hold out much longer. So he sees no point in waiting patiently for a happy ending.

Job feels completely helpless. All his help would have to come from himself, and he has nothing left inside. His wealth, his health and his friends are gone, and any chance of getting through is gone too. Adam Clarke stresses that Job is not losing his mind. He still thinks clearly.

This is Job's main charge against his friends. A man who is falling apart deserves kindness from his friend, even if he has let go of his reverence for God. Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke also take it to mean that a person who refuses pity to a suffering friend has himself let go of the fear of God. Either way, kindness to those in trouble is part of true faith.

Job compares his friends to desert streams that rush and roar in winter, full of melting snow and ice. When summer comes and water is needed most, they shrink and vanish. His friends came with a big show of sympathy, but their help dried up when he needed it. Matthew Henry draws a lesson: people will fail us, but God never runs dry.

Thirsty caravans from Tema and Sheba, two places in hot, dry Arabia, remember water there and go out of their way to find it. They find only dry sand, and some die in the desert. Their high hopes make the letdown even more bitter, and their faces burn with shame. Job had hoped for comfort from his friends in the same way.

Job makes the point plain: like those dry streams, his friends are no help to him at all. They saw how badly he was struck down, and they pulled back in fear. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Job is being gentle here, blaming their fear rather than their hearts. Wesley adds that they may have feared trouble for themselves, or feared that Job would become a burden to them.

Job never asked his friends for money. He never asked them to pay a ransom or to fight the raiders who took his animals. All he wanted was a kind look and a kind word. Even that small thing they did not give.

Job says he is ready to learn. If they show him clearly where he went wrong, he will be quiet and admit it. Honest words carry real force, but their arguments prove nothing. Eliphaz blamed sin but never named a single one.

Job asks why they pick apart the words of a desperate man. Words like that are like wind, gone as soon as they are said. Instead of making allowance for his pain, they pile blame on someone as helpless as an orphan. They treat their friend like something to trade away. Enduring Word notes that Job is hitting back here with sharp charges of his own.

Job begs them to look him in the face. Would he lie to them? He asks them to think again and not judge him unfairly, because his good name before God and people is at stake. Just as the tongue can taste bad food, he can tell if his own words are wrong. He wants them to admit that his suffering is not punishment for some hidden sin.
